name: Remove Leaves In Binary Tree
html:
Welcome back, dear reader. So, are you enjoying the binary tree data structure? We have a lot more in our package for you. So, tighten up your belts and keep moving forward. This question is Remove Leaves Nodes In Binary Tree. What does this question say?


Important Links : Probem Link, Question Video , Solution Video

Problem Discussion :

We have to remove all the leaf nodes from a binary tree. (see fig-1)

You may refer to the question video if you have any doubts about the question. We suggest you try to solve this problem yourself and then go to the solution to verify your method and extract every bit of knowledge out here.

Watch video Approach :

Let us start our discussion with high-level thinking.

High-Level Thinking:
  1. Expectation: We expect that the function removeLeaves() when passed with the root node as a parameter will remove all the leaf nodes from the tree and return the new root node for the tree.
  2. Faith: Have a look at the diagram shown below (fig-2). We have to remove the leaf nodes from the tree. So, we say that if we remove all the leaf nodes from the left subtree and the right subtree then all the leaves will be removed from the tree. We know that you have got some questions. The first one is what if the left child or the right child of the root node is itself a leaf node? Again, have faith over recursion that when we call the recursive function, it will remove the left child or the right child or both, if they are leaf nodes themselves. So, if any child or both the children of the root node are leaf nodes, they themselves get removed.
    What if there is no left child or there is no right child for the root node? Well, if there is no left child for any node, then it does not have any left sub-tree. Then, we don't need to remove anything and the same is the case with the right child. So, if there is a node with only one child, the other sub-tree of that node will not exist and we do not need to make any changes to it.
    The final question is what if the root node does not have both the left and the right children? In that case, the root node is itself a leaf node and it will be removed from the tree and the root of the tree will become null.
    So, our faith is that when we call upon the recursive function for the left child and the right child of a node, the function can handle all these situations and remove the leaf nodes. How will the function handle these situations? We will understand it in the low level thinking process.
  3. Relation: Now we have to finally think of a relation between our expectation and faith. We said that the function is expected to remove leaf nodes and return the new root node after removing the leaves. Have a look at fig-3. According to our faith this should happen (see fig-3). The leaf nodes are removed from the left subtree and the right subtree and we have a new left root for the left subtree and the new right-root for the right sub-tree. This new left root should get attached to the left of the root node and the new right root should get attached to the right of the root node. Therefore, recurrence relation will be:
    node.left=removeLeaves(node.left)
    node.right=removeLeaves(node.right)     So, now we have a relationship too. We have now done the entire procedure of high-level thinking. So, we can now write some code based on the high level thinking and then think about the base case and handling it using the low-level thinking.
    So, dear reader, hope you have understood the high level thinking of the code. The code till the high level thinking is written and explained in the solution video. You may refer to it if you have any doubts about it. Now, let us do the low-level thinking and talk about the base case.
    Watch video
Low-Level Thinking:

Let us begin from the root node and trace the Euler path. We also recommend you to write the code based on high level thinking on your own and keep it by your side for understanding the low-level analysis. So, let us begin. We start from the root node and check whether it is a leaf node or not. Since it is not a leaf node a call is made to the left child of the root node. So, we move to its left child.

Now we are the node (20). Since it is also not a leaf node, a call is made to its left child and we again move forward in the Euler path.

Now we are at node (40). It has no left child and right child. So, it is a leaf node. We have to remove it. But the question is how? How are we going to remove a leaf node?

Have a look at the recurrence relation that we wrote in the code above. We are storing the node that we get from the recursive call into the left child of the parent node. Did you get it? See, we are at a leaf node (40). This is the left child of the node (20). When we remove this leaf node, the new root should be assigned to the left child of the node (20). We also know that if we remove node (40) then there will not be any node at the left of node (20). So, the left child of node (20) should be null.

So, when we are at a leaf node, let us return null from there. This null will be stored in the corresponding child of the parent node (see fig-6).

Now node (40) which was a leaf node is removed from the tree. So we have a base case. But we will trace the Euler path further as we have another base case also. So, we are at node (20) now. We have received the new left root=null and we have successfully removed the leaf node(s) from the left subtree of the node (20). So now the call will be made for its right child. Since the right child exists, we will move to its right child in the Euler path.

When we reach the root 50, we see that it is not a leaf node (since both children are not null). So, a call is made to the left child of node (50). But, there is no left child for node (50). So the call will be made to a null node. If we continue after this an exception will occur. So, this is the other base case we encountered. So, whenever we hit a node which is null, we will return null again indicating that there is no node here. So these are the two base cases:

Base Cases:
  1. When we arrive at a Leaf Node: return null
  2. When we arrive at a Null Node: return null

So, this is the complete procedure with both high-level and low-level thinking. Now that we know the base case too, let's write the complete code.

import java.io.*; import java.util.*; public class Main { public static class Node { int data; Node left; Node right; Node(int data, Node left, Node right) { this.data = data; this.left = left; this.right = right; } } public static class Pair { Node node; int state; Pair(Node node, int state) { this.node = node; this.state = state; } } public static Node construct(Integer[] arr) { Node root = new Node(arr[0], null, null); Pair rtp = new Pair(root, 1); Stack< Pair> st = new Stack< >(); st.push(rtp); int idx = 0; while (st.size() > 0) { Pair top = st.peek(); if (top.state == 1) { idx++; if (arr[idx] != null) { top.node.left = new Node(arr[idx], null, null); Pair lp = new Pair(top.node.left, 1); st.push(lp); } else { top.node.left = null; } top.state++; } else if (top.state == 2) { idx++; if (arr[idx] != null) { top.node.right = new Node(arr[idx], null, null); Pair rp = new Pair(top.node.right, 1); st.push(rp); } else { top.node.right = null; } top.state++; } else { st.pop(); } } return root; } public static void display(Node node) { if (node == null) { return; } String str = ""; str += node.left == null ? "." : node.left.data + ""; str += " <- " + node.data + " -> "; str += node.right == null ? "." : node.right.data + ""; System.out.println(str); display(node.left); display(node.right); } public static Node removeLeaves(Node node){ if(node == null){ return null; } if(node.left == null && node.right == null){ return null; } node.left = removeLeaves(node.left); node.right = removeLeaves(node.right); return node; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in)); int n = Integer.parseInt(br.readLine()); Integer[] arr = new Integer[n]; String[] values = br.readLine().split(" "); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { if (values[i].equals("n") == false) { arr[i] = Integer.parseInt(values[i]); } else { arr[i] = null; } } Node root = construct(arr); root = removeLeaves(root); display(root); } }
java; true";

So, dear reader, we hope that you understood the above code and procedure completely. If you still have any doubts, you may refer to the complete solution video to clear all your doubts. Now let us discuss the time and space complexity of the solution.

Watch video Analysis Time Complexity:

The time complexity of the above solution is O(n) as we are visiting every node in the tree to check whether it is a leaf node or not.

Space Complexity:

The space complexity of the above solution is O(1) as we are not using any extra data structure or memory. If we consider the recursion space then the time complexity of the above solution will become O(log2n) as the maximum height of the stack at any point of time will be O(log2n) which is also the height of the tree.



With this we have solved and understood this problem completely. If you still have any doubts we suggest you refer to the complete solution video to clear them.
